short: Possibly the Althing, Iceland’s historic general assembly.
note: Possibly Iceland’s Alþingi, established around 930 at Þingvellir. Its name combines words for the whole community and an assembly, and the institution became Iceland’s parliament.

short: Thucydides’ debate about power, justice, and submission.
note: In book V of the History of the Peloponnesian War, Athenian envoys demand the surrender of neutral Melos. The dialogue confronts arguments about justice and hope with the demands of superior force.

sources.label: Thucydides: Melian Dialogue, University of North Carolina Wilmington

short: Greek historian of the Peloponnesian War.
note: A fifth-century BCE historian whose account of the conflict between Athens and Sparta examines political judgment, war, and imperial power. His work includes the Melian Dialogue.

sources.label: Thucydides: Melian Dialogue, University of North Carolina Wilmington

short: Bruce Catton, historian of the American Civil War.
note: American writer, 1899–1978, known for narrative histories of the Civil War. A Stillness at Appomattox, concluding his Army of the Potomac trilogy, won the Pulitzer Prize.

sources.label: Case Western Reserve University: Bruce Catton

short: Carl von Clausewitz, author of On War.
note: Prussian soldier and theorist, 1780–1831. His unfinished treatise On War examines the relationship between military action and politics, along with uncertainty, chance, and friction in warfare.

short: The 1862 American Civil War battle near Sharpsburg, Maryland.
note: Fought on 17 September 1862 between Union and Confederate forces. The battle produced the bloodiest single day in American military history and ended Lee’s first invasion of the North.

short: An apparent choice with only one acceptable option.
note: A take-it-or-leave-it offer: the supposed freedom to choose is restricted to accepting what is available or receiving nothing. The phrase traditionally refers to Cambridge carrier Thomas Hobson’s horse-hiring rule.

short: A protective line intended to contain a threat.
note: French for sanitary cordon: originally a guarded boundary restricting movement to contain disease. Figuratively, a barrier of territory, institutions, or forces intended to isolate a dangerous influence.

short: Tchaikovsky and his Christmas ballet, The Nutcracker.
note: A ballet first performed in 1892, with music by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. A girl, often called Clara, receives a nutcracker that becomes central to a magical adventure.

aliases: Piano Concerto No. 2 in C Minor
short: Rachmaninoff and his Second Piano Concerto.
note: Russian composer and pianist, 1873–1943. His Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor, Op. 18, completed in 1901, is known for expansive melodies and the dialogue between virtuoso piano and orchestra.

sources.label: Los Angeles Philharmonic: Piano Concerto No. 2

short: George Gershwin, American composer and pianist.
note: Composer, 1898–1937, who brought jazz and popular-song idioms into concert music. His works include Rhapsody in Blue, An American in Paris, and the opera Porgy and Bess.

sources.label: Library of Congress: George and Ira Gershwin

short: Johannes Brahms, German Romantic composer.
note: Composer and pianist, 1833–1897, whose symphonies, concertos, chamber music, and songs combine Romantic expression with tightly worked classical forms.

short: A mathematical surface with one side and one boundary.
note: A Möbius strip is made by giving a strip a half twist before joining its ends. Named after mathematician August Ferdinand Möbius, it is a basic example of a nonorientable surface.

sources.label: University of St Andrews: Möbius surface

short: Buckminster Fuller’s unfolded-polyhedron map projection.
note: The Dymaxion map associated with designer R. Buckminster Fuller represents Earth on an unfolded polyhedron. Its arrangement emphasizes the connectedness of the continents and avoids a mandatory north-up orientation.

short: An equal-area, often heart-shaped map projection.
note: A pseudoconical projection with concentric circular parallels. Areas are preserved; its overall outline depends on the chosen standard parallel.

sources.label: US Geological Survey: Map Projections—A Working Manual

short: A world map drawn within a circle.
note: A compromise projection that places the world in a circle. It preserves neither area nor local shape and greatly enlarges polar regions.

sources.label: US Geological Survey: Map Projections—A Working Manual

short: An equal-area world map often divided into lobes.
note: John Paul Goode’s combination of sinusoidal and Mollweide projections. Interruptions reduce distortion across selected land or ocean regions.

sources.label: US Geological Survey: Map Projections—A Working Manual

short: A map projection that makes great circles straight.
note: A projection from a sphere’s center onto a tangent plane. Great-circle routes appear as straight lines, with rapidly increasing distortion away from the center.

sources.label: US Geological Survey: Map Projections—A Working Manual

short: A rectangular compromise world-map projection.
note: Osborn Miller’s modification of the Mercator construction. It reduces polar exaggeration while sacrificing Mercator’s preservation of local angles.

sources.label: US Geological Survey: Map Projections—A Working Manual

short: A bright nearby star in the constellation Lyra.
note: One of the three stars of the Summer Triangle, about 25 light-years from Earth. Its brightness and well-studied spectrum have made it an important astronomical reference star.

short: A luminous star in Cygnus, the Swan.
note: The brightest star in Cygnus and one corner of the Summer Triangle. Its name comes from an Arabic word for tail, referring to its place in the constellation.

short: The fraction of incoming light reflected by a surface.
note: A measure of reflectivity, expressed between zero and one or as a percentage. Snow and bright clouds have high albedo; dark ocean water and forests generally reflect much less light.

short: Possibly Marcus Tullius Cicero, Roman orator and statesman.
note: Possibly Marcus Tullius Cicero, 106–43 BCE, the Roman lawyer, politician, and philosophical writer. His speeches and prose became influential models of Latin eloquence.

short: A Roman name for the ruler of the underworld.
note: Dis, or Dis Pater, was identified with Pluto and the Greek Hades. The name links the god to wealth beneath the earth; Latin poetry also uses it for the realm of the dead.

sources.label: Ancient sources on Hades and Dis, collected by Theoi

short: The snake-haired Gorgon whose gaze turned people to stone.
note: One of the three Gorgon sisters in Greek mythology, and the only mortal among them. Perseus killed her by avoiding her direct gaze; her severed head retained its petrifying power.

sources.label: Ancient sources on Medusa, collected by Theoi

short: The courtier beneath a sword suspended by a horsehair.
note: In Cicero’s account, Dionysius lets the admiring Damocles experience royal luxury, then hangs a sword above him by a single horsehair. The episode illustrates the constant insecurity accompanying power.

short: Latin for eagle.
note: The Latin noun aquila means eagle. It also names the eagle-shaped standard carried by a Roman legion and the constellation traditionally pictured as an eagle.

short: Latin for horse.
note: The Latin noun equus means a horse, steed, or charger. It is the source of English words such as equine and equestrian.

short: Roman historian of the early emperors.
note: Publius Cornelius Tacitus, a senator and historian active in the late first and early second centuries CE. His Annals and Histories examine imperial power, political violence, and the loss of republican freedom.

short: An oblique equal-area map projection.
note: William Briesemeister’s modification of the Hammer projection, presented in 1953. It places the globe obliquely within an ellipse, preserving relative areas while altering shapes.

sources.label: US Geological Survey: An Album of Map Projections

short: Barrie’s never-aging boy and his island, Neverland.
note: The flying boy at the center of Barrie’s play Peter Pan and novel Peter and Wendy. Neverland is his island of perpetual childhood, shared with the Lost Boys and Captain Hook.

short: Christopher Marlowe, author of Doctor Faustus.
note: Elizabethan playwright whose Doctor Faustus dramatizes a scholar’s bargain with a devil. Mephistophilis explains that separation from divine bliss makes hell a condition he carries with him.

short: Norbert Wiener’s book about cybernetics and religion.
note: Published in 1964, Wiener’s short book considers machines that learn, machines that reproduce, and the ethical relationship between people and their creations. Its questions connect technological agency with religious ideas of creation.

short: Adam’s dream of reality in Milton’s Paradise Lost.
note: In book VIII of Paradise Lost, Adam describes waking to discover that what he dreamed exists. Keats compares imagination to this experience in his letter to Benjamin Bailey of 22 November 1817.

sources.label: Cowper & Newton Museum: Keats and Adam’s dream

term: May there not be superior beings
short: From Keats’s letter of 19 March 1819.
note: In a journal-letter to George and Georgiana Keats, the poet compares human purposes with animal instinct. He wonders whether higher beings might appreciate human thought as humans appreciate an animal’s alertness.

sources.label: John Keats: Letters to His Family and Friends

short: Seeking revenge or the recovery of something lost.
note: From French revanche, revenge. In politics it usually describes efforts to reverse a defeat or recover lost territory; more broadly it suggests a determination to reclaim lost power or standing.

short: An old slang word for a prostitute or mistress.
note: Also spelled doxy. A disparaging term found in older English slang for a sex worker or a man’s mistress.

short: Italian for a carriage or vehicle.
note: An Italian word for a vehicle used to carry passengers, historically a horse-drawn carriage and in modern usage also a car or railway carriage.

short: An informal Italian restaurant.
note: An Italian eating house, traditionally more modest and informal than a grand restaurant, serving familiar regional or home-style cooking.

short: In a low, quiet voice.
note: Italian for under the voice. The expression describes subdued speech or singing, often an aside intended to be heard by only a few people.

short: Something already done that others must accept.
note: French for accomplished fact. It describes a completed action or settled situation presented to others before they can meaningfully object or choose an alternative.

short: A person’s double or uncanny look-alike.
note: From German Doppelgänger, literally double-goer. The word can mean a supernatural double or, more loosely, someone who closely resembles another person.

short: A small dart-shaped metal projectile.
note: From French for little arrow. Flechettes are finned metal darts used as projectiles or dispersed from certain shells; the word describes their arrow-like shape.

short: Possibly H. H. Asquith, British prime minister.
note: Possibly Herbert Henry Asquith, 1852–1928, Liberal prime minister from 1908 to 1916. His government pursued major constitutional and welfare reforms and led Britain into the First World War.

short: Possibly the celebrated river valley in ancient Thessaly.
note: Possibly the Vale of Tempe in Greece, where the Peneios River passes between Mount Olympus and Mount Ossa on its way to the sea. Ancient writers praised the wooded valley’s beauty.

sources.label: Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography: Tempe

short: Possibly Mount Fuji, Japan’s sacred volcanic mountain.
note: Possibly Mount Fuji, the volcano on Honshu whose symmetrical profile is a familiar subject of Japanese art. Long a place of pilgrimage, it anchors the Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park.

sources.label: Japan Ministry of the Environment: Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park

short: Latin forms meaning peace.
note: Pacem is the accusative singular of Latin pax, peace. The form appears in dona nobis pacem, grant us peace, and Pacem in terris, peace on earth.

short: Possibly two Chinese place names: Qingdao and Xishuangbanna.
note: Possibly a combination of older romanizations of Qingdao, a coastal city in Shandong, and Xishuangbanna, a region of southern Yunnan bordering Laos and Myanmar. The two names refer to geographically distant places.

sources.label: University of Toronto: historical and modern place-name concordance

short: Possibly T. H. White’s Merlyn, who lives backward through time.
note: Possibly the version of Arthur’s wizard in T. H. White’s The Sword in the Stone and The Once and Future King. Merlyn experiences time backward, remembering events that other people regard as the future.

sources.label: University of Glasgow: T. H. White’s The Sword in the Stone

short: Thomas Aquinas, medieval philosopher and theologian.
note: Dominican thinker, c. 1225–1274, whose work joins Christian theology with sustained engagement with Aristotle. His Summa theologiae examines God, human conduct, and salvation through systematic questions and arguments.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas

short: Capable of moving independently.
note: Able to move spontaneously or under its own power, especially as a living organism does.

short: A dry watercourse or steep-sided gully.
note: A channel or ravine in an arid region, commonly dry except after rainfall.

short: A rigid or distorted grin.
note: A gaping mouth or an expression resembling a fixed, strained grin.

short: A doughnut-shaped surface or solid.
note: In geometry, the ring-shaped surface produced by revolving a circle around an axis outside the circle but in its plane.

short: Melting or dissolving away.
note: Becoming liquid or disappearing as if by melting; technically, dissolving through the absorption of moisture from the air.

short: Outlandish or strikingly unconventional.
note: Exceeding accepted standards of style or behavior; conspicuously unusual or bizarre.

short: An old name for certain fragrant garden flowers.
note: An old name for carnations.

short: Archaic: lovers or sweethearts.
note: An old word for a lover or sweetheart, especially a mistress.

short: A bowl for a festive spiced drink.
note: Wassail is a drink traditionally made from warmed ale, wine, or cider with spices and other ingredients, shared in toasts and seasonal celebrations.

short: Strongly scented or suggestive of something.
note: Having a noticeable fragrance; figuratively, evoking or calling something to mind.

short: Changes of circumstance or fortune.
note: Alternations and fluctuations in life or events, especially unwelcome or unpredictable changes.

short: An artist’s or writer’s body of work.
note: The collected works of an artist, writer, or composer; the word can also denote an individual artistic work.

short: Made concrete or treated as a tangible thing.
note: Converted into something concrete, or regarded as a real thing rather than an abstraction.

short: Sailing vessels; also spelled barques.
note: A poetic name for boats or ships; more specifically, a sailing ship with three or more masts, square-rigged except for its aftermost mast.

short: A smokeless propellant used in firearms and artillery.
note: A propellant made chiefly from nitrocellulose and nitroglycerin, traditionally formed into cords.

short: Fine spray swept along by the wind.
note: Spray blown from wave crests, or similarly wind-driven snow or sand.

short: Ancient warships with three banks of oars.
note: Oared warships used in the ancient Mediterranean, with rowers arranged in three levels.

short: Fine particles dispersed through another substance.
note: A mixture in which very small particles remain distributed through a surrounding medium rather than forming a true solution.

short: Relating to an elite bodyguard, especially an emperor’s.
note: The Praetorian Guard protected Roman emperors. The adjective can more generally describe a ruler’s privileged military guard.

short: Conventionally, the plane of Earth’s orbit around the Sun.
note: In conventional Earth-based astronomy, the ecliptic is the Sun’s apparent yearly path across the sky. Its plane corresponds to Earth’s orbital plane and serves as an astronomical reference.

short: A glow caused by electrical discharge into the air.
note: A luminous plasma discharge around exposed points such as ship masts or aircraft wings in a strong atmospheric electric field. It often appears blue or violet.

sources.label: Hong Kong Observatory: St. Elmo’s fire

short: The site of a Greek–Persian naval battle in 480 BCE.
note: A headland on northern Euboea, off which the allied Greek fleet fought Xerxes’ Persian fleet while the land battle at Thermopylae was taking place.

short: From Keats’s comic portrait of Charles Armitage Brown.
note: From “Spenserian Stanzas on Charles Armitage Brown,” also known as “Character of Charles Brown,” a humorous poem by John Keats about his friend.

sources.label: John Keats: Spenserian Stanzas on Charles Armitage Brown

short: A cylindrical map projection with a rectangular grid.
note: A projection mapping meridians and parallels to evenly spaced straight lines. The grid becomes square in the plate carrée form, whose standard parallel is the equator.

short: A globe-like map projection viewed from infinitely far away.
note: An azimuthal projection displaying one hemisphere as it would appear from an infinite viewing distance. Distortion increases toward its circular edge.

short: An equal-area map projection with curved meridians.
note: A pseudocylindrical projection with straight, equally spaced parallels and sinusoidally curved meridians. It preserves areas but increasingly distorts shapes away from its center.

short: A map projection preserving distance and direction from its center.
note: A projection in which distances and directions measured from the central point are correct. Other distances and shapes become increasingly distorted away from that point.

short: A map projection using a separate conical surface for each parallel.
note: A projection with parallels drawn as arcs of different circles, as though each lay on its own cone. Scale is true along each parallel and the central meridian.

short: Aggressive, warlike nationalism.
note: Exaggerated patriotism marked by a belligerent attitude toward other nations.

short: A small, slender member of the weasel family.
note: The ermine, especially when wearing its brown summer coat rather than its white winter fur.

short: Bile-colored or sickly in appearance.
note: Relating to bile, the yellow-green digestive fluid; also describing a sickly or unpleasant appearance, or an irritable disposition.

short: Daily, or occurring during daylight.
note: Relating to the day or recurring every day; in biology, active chiefly during daylight.

short: Relating to extremely low temperatures.
note: Concerning the production and effects of very low temperatures, or processes carried out under such conditions.

short: A hard protective outer shell.
note: The protective shell covering the back of such animals as turtles and crustaceans; by extension, a shell-like covering or armor.

short: Granted or bestowed as a favor.
note: Given or allowed by someone in a position of authority, often with an implication of graciousness or condescension.

short: Difficult to understand; obscure.
note: Describes ideas or subjects that are remote from ordinary knowledge and hard to comprehend.

short: Next to last.
note: Immediately preceding the final member in an ordered series.

short: A group of three acting together.
note: Originally a Russian carriage drawn by three horses; by extension, a trio, especially a group sharing leadership.

short: An unexpected outside agency that resolves a difficulty.
note: Latin for “god from the machine,” originally a deity lowered onto the stage in ancient drama. It now denotes an improbable external intervention that solves a plot’s problem.

short: A drink mixing two kinds of beer in equal parts.
note: A mixture of equal quantities of two kinds of malt beverage, such as dark and light beer.

short: Holy Communion, or its consecrated bread and wine.
note: The Christian sacrament commemorating the Last Supper; the term also denotes the consecrated elements used in it.

short: The Roman Catholic religious order known as the Jesuits.
note: The order founded by Ignatius of Loyola and his companions and approved in 1540, known for education, missionary work, and spiritual formation.

short: Tapering map segments used to cover a globe.
note: Strips carrying map information, shaped to fit around a spherical globe. They are typically widest at the equator and narrow toward the poles.

sources.label: Oxford History of Science Museum: make a model globe
Oxford History of Science Museum: gores for a terrestrial globe

short: A mixture assembled from different elements or styles.
note: A work made from varied borrowed elements, or one imitating another work’s style; more broadly, a miscellaneous mixture.

short: The attendants accompanying an important person.
note: A group of assistants, followers, or servants who travel with or attend someone of rank.

short: Aristocratic in appearance or manner.
note: Associated with hereditary high rank or refined social standing; originally referring to the privileged families of ancient Rome.

short: Howled or wailed with a wavering sound.
note: Uttered a prolonged, rising-and-falling cry or howl.

short: Defensive walls or embankments.
note: Broad raised defenses of earth or masonry surrounding a fortified place, often carrying a parapet.

short: Compartments for passengers, engines, or equipment on an aircraft.
note: A streamlined enclosure for an aircraft’s engine, crew, or other equipment; also the passenger compartment beneath an airship.

short: Herring preserved by splitting, salting, and smoking.
note: Fish, especially herring, split open, cured with salt, and usually smoked before being eaten.

short: People given to coarse or indecent speech.
note: An older spelling of the plural noun ribald: a person who uses vulgar, lewd, or coarse language.

short: A vivid, deep blue.
note: A rich blue pigment originally made from lapis lazuli, or the color of that pigment.

short: A metrical foot with two stressed syllables.
note: In accentual verse, a foot consisting of two stressed syllables; in classical quantitative verse, two long syllables.

short: A metrical foot with two unstressed syllables.
note: In poetry, a foot of two unstressed syllables, or two short syllables in classical quantitative meter.

short: A pause within a line of verse.
note: A pause or break within a verse line, often arising from the sense or punctuation; conventionally marked in scansion by a double vertical line.

short: The repetition of vowel sounds.
note: The recurrence of similar vowel sounds in nearby words, especially their stressed syllables, without requiring full rhyme.

short: Using an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
note: Describes verse built from iambs: two-syllable feet with the weaker or unstressed syllable before the stronger or stressed one.

short: The practice of seeking converts.
note: The effort to convert others to a religion, belief, or cause.

short: Conflict within a group; mutually destructive.
note: Describes strife between members of the same group, or fighting destructive to both sides.

short: A religious ascetic or renunciant.
note: Sanskrit śramaṇa, corresponding to Pali samaṇa: a religious seeker who leaves ordinary social life for disciplined spiritual practice, including Buddhist and Jain ascetics.

short: A carrier of the strong nuclear interaction.
note: An elementary force-carrying particle associated with the strong interaction, which binds quarks together.

short: A paradoxical saying or question used in Zen practice.
note: A brief, often perplexing question or saying used in Zen training to challenge ordinary reasoning and prompt insight.

short: A Nazi forced-labor and punishment camp in Essen.
note: A school building in Essen used from 1943 to hold forced laborers and, from 1944, as a punitive labor camp run by the Gestapo and the Krupp firm.

sources.label: Essen City Archive · Essen Erinnert, station 3.2

short: The opening of a short lyric by John Keats.
note: A short lyric by John Keats. Its two stanzas address a spirit first through suffering and mourning, then through laughter and festive revelry.

sources.label: University of Victoria · Mapping Keats’s Progress

short: A spring-deposited limestone used in buildings.
note: A form of limestone formed by calcium-carbonate deposits from springs, particularly hot springs, and widely used as an ornamental building stone.

short: Suggesting a return to an ancestral condition.
note: Reverting to, or recalling, characteristics of a remote ancestor or an earlier form of life.

short: Pole weapons combining an axe blade and spear point.
note: Long-shafted weapons with an axe-like blade, a pointed hook or beak, and a spear point at the top.

short: Upright supports beneath a railing.
note: A row of closely spaced posts or spindles supporting a handrail; an individual support is a baluster.

short: Bearlike.
note: Of, resembling, or characteristic of a bear.

short: A fever marked by chills and shivering.
note: An older term for recurrent fever and shaking chills, especially malarial fever; also used more broadly of a shivering fit.

short: Patterned fabric, or a grayish-red color.
note: A lustrous woven fabric with contrasting patterns; also a grayish-red color, or an adjective for something of that color.

short: Temples or shrines.
note: An archaic or poetic word for temples, shrines, or churches.

short: A low, usually moist hollow in the land.
note: A shallow depression or valley-like hollow, often wetter and more thickly vegetated than the surrounding ground.

short: A stand supporting a body or coffin before burial.
note: A frame, platform, or stand on which a corpse or coffin rests before burial.

short: A traditional size or type of writing paper.
note: Writing or printing paper named for a fool’s-cap watermark formerly used on it; traditionally a British sheet about 13½ by 17 inches.

short: The central administration of the Roman Catholic Church.
note: The Roman Curia: the papal court and governing offices through which the pope administers the Church.

short: Maintenance of stable internal conditions.
note: The regulation of an organism’s internal environment, such as temperature and fluid chemistry, through responses that counter disruptive changes.

short: Absorption in one’s own experience.
note: Extreme preoccupation with one’s own feelings; in philosophy, the position that only one’s own mind exists or can be known to exist.

short: A song or expression of praise.
note: An enthusiastic tribute or song of praise; originally a hymn invoking or thanking an ancient Greek deity.

short: A commotion or fuss.
note: An older word for bustle, agitation, fuss, or uproar.

short: A bacterium, especially one shaped like a rod.
note: A term for a rod-shaped bacterium, formerly also used more generally for bacteria.

short: Debris or discarded remains.
note: Loose fragments, debris, or waste left after something breaks down or is used; in geology, particles worn from rock.

short: In extreme distress or near death.
note: A Latin phrase meaning in desperate circumstances or at the point of death.

short: A question-and-answer exchange in Zen teaching.
note: A dialogue between a Zen teacher and a questioner, often using unexpected replies to challenge habitual understanding.

sources.label: D. T. Suzuki · Manual of Zen Buddhism, Chinese Zen Masters

short: Zhuangzi, in the famous butterfly-dream story.
note: In chapter 2 of the Zhuangzi, the philosopher dreams he is a butterfly and then wonders whether he is a butterfly dreaming of being Zhuangzi.

short: Writing formed from wedge-shaped signs.
note: An ancient writing system that developed in Mesopotamia, using impressed wedge-shaped signs on clay. It was adapted to write numerous languages.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Cuneiform tablet

short: Historical Italian coins or monetary units.
note: Plural of scudo, a name used for various gold or silver coins and monetary units in the Italian states.

short: The countryside surrounding Rome.
note: The Roman Campagna, the rural country around Rome, long celebrated in literature and landscape painting.

short: Lionlike.
note: Resembling or characteristic of a lion.

short: Humanlike or apelike.
note: Resembling a human or an ape; also a zoological term relating to monkeys, apes, and humans.

short: Affected by tuberculosis.
note: An older medical adjective for someone suffering from consumption, especially tuberculosis of the lungs.

short: Dead or dying tissue.
note: Describes animal or plant tissue that is dead or undergoing tissue death.

short: Literally, having an unusually small head.
note: A medical and anatomical adjective for a head with an abnormally small braincase.

short: Producing light through biological processes.
note: Emitting light through chemical reactions in a living organism, as in fireflies or some marine animals.

short: Exceptionally luminous galactic centers.
note: Bright active galactic nuclei powered by matter falling toward supermassive black holes; their radiation can outshine the surrounding galaxy.

short: Places where relativity’s description of spacetime breaks down.
note: In general relativity, irregular boundaries where spacetime ends, often associated with unbounded curvature. Their appearance in the theory signals limits to its physical description.

short: A close association between different kinds of organisms.
note: Living together in a close relationship, which may be mutually beneficial, neutral, or parasitic; also used of interdependent people or groups.

short: A state that can involve stupor and muscular rigidity.
note: A syndrome affecting movement and responsiveness, often involving marked immobility or stupor and sometimes alternating with agitation.

short: Energy units equal to a billion electronvolts each.
note: A gigaelectronvolt, abbreviated GeV, is one billion electronvolts, a unit commonly used for energies in particle physics.

short: Mozart’s solo-piano fantasia, K. 397.
note: A piano work by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, probably left as a fragment. The familiar closing bars come from an unauthorized 1806 edition, with no surviving authorized version by Mozart.

sources.label: G. Henle Verlag · Mozart, Fantasy in D minor

short: Theories uniting the electromagnetic and nuclear forces.
note: A grand unified theory seeks a common mathematical description of electromagnetism and the strong and weak nuclear interactions, with a shared behavior at sufficiently high energies.

short: French: above; En Avant: forward.
note: En Haut means above or on high; En Avant means forward or ahead. These paired directions recur in accounts of Teilhard de Chardin’s spiritual thought.

sources.label: F.-M. Bergounioux · L’âme sacerdotale de Teilhard de Chardin

short: Journals that attacked Keats’s Endymion.
note: Blackwood’s Edinburgh Magazine, the Quarterly Review, and the British Critic printed hostile reviews of Endymion in 1818. The Blackwood’s notice was by John Gibson Lockhart; the Quarterly’s was by John Wilson Croker.

sources.label: University of Victoria · Keats and the hostile reviews of 1818

short: A playful poem by John Keats.
note: The recurring opening of Keats’s comic poem about a restless boy travelling north to Scotland; the quoted stanza follows his urge to write poetry.

sources.label: University of Victoria · Keats, There was a naughty boy

short: Keats and Severn’s landlady in Rome.
note: The landlady who occupied the rear rooms of the apartment at the Spanish Steps while John Keats and Joseph Severn stayed in its front rooms during Keats’s final illness.

sources.label: Amy Weldon · Keats-Shelley House, The Common
